system:
You are the Met office reviewer, standing in for the national meteorological centre (hazard facts). You check that the alert says what the hazard bulletin says: the same hazard, the same times, the same places, severity and certainty no higher or lower than the bulletin supports, and no unverified report in the alert.
You see only the event inputs (marked verified or unverified) and the English alert fields. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

[MHEWS-2026#0379] Leveraging AI to Enhance Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems (full report) (p.95):
Techniques such as text mining, topic modelling, and Named Entity Recognition are widely used for sentiment and emotion analysis across disasters including floods, hurricanes, typhoons, and snowstorms. Although research is extensive, operational application in early warning systems remains limited. NLP-based sentiment analysis can reveal when warning messages lack clarity or empathy, affecting communication effectiveness, and help authorities refine future messaging and communication strategies (Salley et al., 2025). AI for detecting and mitigating disaster misinformation Misinformation is a significant challenge during disasters. False or misleading information may include rumours, unverified reports, exaggerated hazard impacts (such as false earthquake predictions), or fraudulent aid claims (Komendantova & Erokhin, 2025). Such misinformation can generate confusion and panic, discourage affected populations from seeking assistance, and disrupt relief and rescue operations. To address this, NLP and machine-learning approaches are being developed to detect and mitigate false information. For example, sentiment analysis can identify sudden surges in negative discourse linked to misinformation spread (Komendantova & Erokhin, 2025), while deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks, are used to detect manipulated or fake images (Hamid et al., 2023). The effectiveness of AI-based misinformation management relies on digital data. Many AI approaches rely on large volumes of information from online platforms such as social media, messaging services, and digital news sources.

data.summary: The fog content matches the NCM bulletin: the hazard, times (21:30 Tue 17 Feb to 10:00 Wed 18 Feb), western regions, Moderate severity and Likely certainty all fit. However, the description adds a dam-burst report near Al Ain with an evacuation order. No input supports this report, and it is a second hazard. It must be removed.

objections.issue: The description includes a dam-burst report and evacuation order near Al Ain. No event input supports it: the only verified hazard input is the NCM fog warning. It is also a second event inside a fog alert.
objections.fix: Delete the sentence 'Reports say a dam near Al Ain has burst; leave the area now.' Keep the description limited to the NCM fog warning. If a dam incident is confirmed by the responsible authority, it needs its own separate alert.
